title: The planning horizon and choosing management stages
blurb: Explain why PRINCE2 plans in detail only for the near future, and what decides the number and length of management stages.
question: Why does PRINCE2 use a high-level project plan together with a detailed stage plan for the current stage, rather than one detailed plan for the whole project?

teach.body: Formally, the planning horizon is the period of time for which it is possible to plan accurately. Only the near future can be planned in detail; beyond it, estimates become less reliable. Plain English: you can say exactly what the team will do next month, but only roughly what it will do next year. PRINCE2 therefore plans the near future in detail and the rest at a higher level.

teach.caption: The detail available drops the further ahead you look, so the detailed stage plan is prepared close to when its work happens.

teach.body: Because of the planning horizon, PRINCE2 combines a high-level project plan covering the whole project with a detailed stage plan for the current stage only. Each later stage plan is produced near the end of the stage before it, when the project manager knows enough to plan it properly. This is how the plans practice supports the manage by stages principle.

A management stage is a section of the project that the project manager manages on behalf of the board, ending with a decision point. The number and length of stages depend on the planning horizon, where key decisions are needed, the level of risk and the complexity of the project. There must be at least two: the initiation stage, then one or more delivery stages. Stage ends can also be aligned with external events, such as the business's budget cycle.

teach.caption: Shorter stages give the board more control; longer stages reduce the burden on senior management. Balance them for the project's size, risk and complexity.
In an iterative-incremental project, quality and acceptance criteria can be refined stage by stage alongside the products, using a product backlog.
Each stage end is a point where the board reviews viability and decides whether to continue. Closure runs inside the final stage.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Brackenford Museum's new gallery
teach.body: At Brackenford Museum, project manager Anika Shah plans a new gallery. The building works carry most of the risk, and the trustees' funding is confirmed each April. She proposes initiation, a design stage ending in March so the board can decide before the funding round, a build stage, then a fit-out stage that includes closure. Executive Owen Clarke agrees: the stage ends fall at genuine decision points and keep detailed planning within a sensible horizon.

teach.text: Every PRINCE2 project has at least two stages, and the first is always initiation. Closing a project is not a stage: it happens inside the final delivery stage. More stages are not automatically better; each adds board effort, so the number should reflect the planning horizon, decision points, risk and complexity.

items: Planning horizon: only the near future can be planned in detail (7.2.1).
So PRINCE2 uses a high-level project plan plus a detailed stage plan for the current stage.
Number and length of stages depend on planning horizon, decision points, risk and complexity (7.2.3).
Minimum two stages; a simple project may need only initiation plus one delivery stage.
Shorter stages = more board control; longer stages = less burden on senior management.

summary: You can now explain the planning horizon and why it leads to a high-level project plan plus detailed stage plans. You can also describe how the number and length of management stages are chosen, from a minimum of two, against the planning horizon, decision points, risk and complexity.

A.q: Which statement describes the planning horizon?
options: The date by which the project plan must be baselined
The period for which it is possible to plan accurately
The final date in the project's time tolerance
The point at which the project board reviews the stage
A.why: The planning horizon is the period for which accurate planning is possible; only the near future can be planned in detail (7.2.1).

whyNot.0: Baselining the project plan happens when the board authorizes the project; that is not the planning horizon.
whyNot.2: Time tolerance limits how far a target date may move; it is not the planning horizon.
whyNot.3: Board reviews happen at stage ends; the horizon is about how far ahead detail is reliable.

A.q: What is the minimum number of management stages in a PRINCE2 project?
options: One
Three
Four
Two
A.why: There must be at least two stages: the initiation stage and at least one delivery stage (7.2.3).

whyNot.0: A single stage would leave no separate initiation before delivery begins.
whyNot.1: Three is common but not the minimum; a simple project can use two.
whyNot.2: Four is not a minimum; the number depends on the project.

A.q: Which is the first stage of every PRINCE2 project?
options: The initiation stage
The design stage
The first delivery stage
The starting up stage
A.why: The first management stage is always the initiation stage (2.4, 7.2.3).

whyNot.1: A design stage is a possible delivery stage in some projects, not a fixed first stage.
whyNot.3: Starting up a project is a pre-project process, not a management stage.

B.q:
Which two factors are used to decide the number and length of management stages?
1. The planning horizon.
2. The level of risk in the project.
3. The number of team managers available.
4. The frequency of checkpoint reports.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: The number and length of stages depend on the planning horizon, decision points, risk and complexity (7.2.3).

whyNot.1: Statement 3 is false: the number of team managers does not decide how stages are set.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is false: checkpoint frequency is set in each work package, not used to define stages.
whyNot.3: Neither team manager numbers nor checkpoint frequency decide the stages.

B.q: A project board wants more frequent opportunities to review viability on a high-risk project. What is the likely effect on the stages?
options: Longer stages, so the board meets less often
Shorter stages, giving more decision points
A single delivery stage to reduce reporting
Removing the initiation stage to save time
B.why: Shorter stages give the board more control and more decision points; longer stages reduce the burden on senior management (2.4, 7.2.3).

whyNot.0: Longer stages reduce the number of decision points, the opposite of what the board wants.
whyNot.2: One delivery stage gives fewer review points, which suits simple, low-risk projects.
whyNot.3: The initiation stage is required in every PRINCE2 project.

B.q: Which project is most likely to need only two management stages?
options: A complex project using several new suppliers
A high-risk project with uncertain requirements
A simple project with few, well-understood products
An iterative project refining its criteria as it goes
B.why: A simple project with a small number of well-understood products and a mature delivery method may need only initiation plus one delivery stage (7.2.3.1).

whyNot.0: Complexity and many suppliers point to more stages and decision points.
whyNot.1: High risk and uncertainty call for shorter stages and more decision points.
whyNot.3: An iterative-incremental project may use several delivery stages while criteria are refined through a product backlog.

C.q: Because of the planning horizon, which pair of plans does PRINCE2 use, and when is each later stage plan prepared?
options: A project plan and a stage plan; during initiation for every stage
A team plan and a stage plan; at the start of each stage
A project plan and a stage plan; near the end of the preceding stage
A project plan and an exception plan; when the board asks
C.why: PRINCE2 uses a high-level project plan and a detailed stage plan for the current stage; later stage plans are prepared near the end of the preceding stage (2.4, 7.2.2.2).

whyNot.0: Planning every stage in detail during initiation ignores the planning horizon.
whyNot.1: Team plans are optional work package plans, and a stage plan is approved before its stage starts.
whyNot.3: Exception plans respond to exceptions; they are not the routine response to the planning horizon.

C.q: An executive suggests ending a stage at the close of the business's financial year. Which statement best supports this?
options: Stage ends can be aligned with external events such as budget cycles
Stage ends are fixed at equal intervals once initiation is complete
Stage ends should match the end of each work package
Stage ends are chosen by team managers to suit their teams
C.why: Stage ends can be aligned with external influences, such as the business's budget-setting cycle, to clarify their impact on the project (2.4).

whyNot.1: Stage lengths vary with the planning horizon, decision points, risk and complexity; they are not set at equal intervals.
whyNot.2: A stage usually contains several work packages; stage ends are about decision points, not each package.
whyNot.3: The project manager decides how stages are applied and the board approves the plans.

C.q: Which is NOT a reason for dividing a project into management stages?
options: To give the board review and decision points
To delegate authority one stage at a time
To keep detailed planning within the horizon
To give each team manager a stage of their own
C.why: Stages provide decision points, delegate authority stage by stage and keep detailed planning near-term (2.4, 7.2.1). Giving each team manager a stage is not a reason; team managers receive work packages.

whyNot.0: Review and decision points are a core reason for stages.
whyNot.1: Delegating authority one stage at a time is how stages support manage by exception.
whyNot.2: The planning horizon is a key reason for stage-by-stage planning.

reteach.title: Weather forecasts and stages
reteach.question: Why does a ten-day weather forecast give hourly detail for tomorrow but only rough outlines for next week?

blocks.body: Forecasters give detail only where it is reliable. Project planning works the same way: the stage plan gives detail for the next stage, and the project plan gives an outline for the rest. When the next stage gets close, it is planned in detail. Stage ends are where the board looks at the latest outlook and decides whether to carry on.

blocks.text: At least two stages, initiation first. Closure sits inside the last stage. Choose the number of stages using the planning horizon, decision points, risk and complexity.

explain.body: Only the near future can be planned in detail. Beyond the planning horizon, plans are kept at a high level until more is known.

test.q: What does the planning horizon mean for the level of detail in plans?
options: All stages are planned in equal detail at initiation
Detail is used for the near future, outline beyond it
Detail is held in team plans for the whole project
Detail is added once a stage has been completed
test.why: Only the near future can be planned in detail, so the current stage is planned in detail and later work in outline (7.2.1).

whyNot.0: Planning all stages in equal detail up front ignores the planning horizon.
whyNot.2: Team plans are optional and cover work packages, not the whole project.
whyNot.3: Detail is needed before the work so it can be controlled, not after the stage ends.

explain.body: Initiation is always the first stage. At least one delivery stage follows. A simple, well-understood project may need just these two.

test.q: A small project uses two management stages. What are they?
options: Starting up and an initiation stage
Initiation and closure
Initiation and one delivery stage
Design and build
test.why: The minimum is the initiation stage plus one delivery stage; closure happens within the delivery stage (7.2.3.1).

whyNot.0: Starting up a project happens before the first stage.
whyNot.1: Closure is not a stage; it is part of the final stage.
whyNot.3: Without initiation first, this is not a PRINCE2 stage structure.

explain.body: Planning horizon, decision points, risk and complexity decide the number and length of stages. Stage ends can be aligned with external events.

test.q: Which factor is used when deciding the length of a management stage?
options: The number of quality reviewers
The size of the change budget
The project's risk appetite statement
Where key decisions are needed
test.why: Stage number and length depend on the planning horizon, decision points, risk and complexity (7.2.3).

whyNot.0: Reviewer numbers relate to quality control, not stage length.
whyNot.1: The change budget funds approved changes; it does not set stages.
whyNot.2: Risk appetite is the business's attitude to risk; the project's level of risk, not the appetite statement, is the stage factor.

explain.body: Shorter stages mean more control and more decision points for the board. Longer stages mean less burden on senior management. Choose to suit the project.

test.q: What is the main benefit of choosing longer management stages?
options: Less burden on senior management
More decision points for the board
More detail in the project plan
Smaller stage tolerances for the PM
test.why: Longer stages reduce the burden on senior management, at the cost of fewer decision points (2.4).

whyNot.1: More decision points come from shorter stages.
whyNot.2: Stage length does not add detail to the high-level project plan.
whyNot.3: Tolerances are set separately by the board; stage length does not shrink them.
